title: Colour (Module 6B, lesson 30)
summary: The 12-hue colour wheel. Primary colours: red, yellow and blue (basis of all other colours). Secondary: orange, green and purple (two primaries mixed in equal quantity). Tertiary: a primary mixed with a secondary in equal quantity (yellow-orange, red-orange, red-purple, blue-purple, blue-green, yellow-green): 3 primary + 3 secondary + 6 tertiary = 12. Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) have fire or sun in them, give warmth, excitement and happiness and reduce visual size; common in traditional Indian embroidery for happy occasions. Cool colours (blue, green, purple) give a cool, peaceful feeling, enhance size and length, are used for summers and balance warm colours. Warm and cool colours are complementary. Neutral colours (white, black, grey, brown, tan, beige) form an effective background for bright colours and are handy when unsure of a scheme. Metallic colours: badla (plain gold or silver wire), kasab (wire wound around a thread), sitara (metal spangles) and mukaish (tiny dots made of badla); today synthetic or 'tested' zari is used.

Hue: the name of the colour. Value: lightness or darkness of a hue; adding white gives a tint (lighter), adding black gives a shade or tone (darker); use a hue with two tints and one tone for natural motifs. Intensity: brightness or dullness; use bright and dull colours in correct proportions; placing complementary colours side by side increases intensity (red and parrot green).

A colour scheme is a pleasing colour combination. Monochromatic: tints and shades of one colour (restful, easiest, always successful; Lucknow chikankari white on white). Analogous (adjacent): neighbouring colours on the wheel with a hue in common (yellow flowers, yellow-green leaves, green stems). Complementary: two colours opposite each other (yellow-purple, orange-blue, red-green, yellow green-red purple, blue green-red orange, blue purple-yellow orange); bright and cheerful, suitable for children's wear and happy occasions; let one colour be prominent. Split complementary: three colours, one colour and the two on either side of its complement (yellow with red-purple and blue-purple). Triad: three colours forming an equilateral triangle (yellow, red, blue or orange, green, purple). Tetrad: four colours forming a square (green, yellow-orange, red, blue-purple), used in Kashida of Jammu and Kashmir, Kantha of Bengal and Chamba Rumal of Himachal. Contrast: striking combinations, complementary colours, light and dark shades; a black or white outline emphasises contrast (white deepens a colour; black lightens and brightens). Harmony: colours from the same area of the wheel (pastel yellow and deep green).
## Significance and factors in the use of colour

Meanings: dark red love, health, vitality; bright red passion, danger; pink femininity and innocence; orange ambition and enthusiasm; brown utility and maturity; yellow inspiration, wisdom and gaiety; dark gold luxury and riches; light yellow and green freshness and youth; blue calmness, sincerity and idealism; purple magnificence and royalty. In the West black is for mourning; in India and China white. Factors: age, sex, profession, occasion, season (cool, soft colours in summer; bright, dark ones in winter), type of garment and body structure of the person. Children and young adults look better in bright colours; older people in colours that suit their responsible image.

vsa: What are neutral colours, and why are they important in embroidery? Explain with an example.
Neutral colours are white, black, grey, brown, tan and beige. They give an effective background for bright colours and are useful when unsure of a scheme, such as white threadwork on a grey fabric.
What are metallic colours? Name two traditional types of metallic wires used in Indian embroidery.
Metallic colours are the sparkle and shimmer of metal used in embroidery. Badla is plain gold or silver wire and kasab is the wire wound around a thread.
Differentiate between warm and cool colours.
Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel warm and exciting and reduce size. Cool colours (blue, green, purple) feel peaceful and increase size.
Define tertiary colours with an example.
They are formed by mixing a primary and a secondary colour in equal quantity, such as blue and green gives blue-green.
What is the difference between a tint and a shade?
A tint is a lighter colour got by adding white to a hue. A shade or tone is a darker colour got by adding black.
sa: Explain complementary and split complementary colour schemes (three points).

(i) A complementary scheme uses two colours opposite each other, such as red and green. (ii) A split complementary scheme uses one colour and the two colours on either side of its complement, such as yellow with red-purple and blue-purple. (iii) Both are bright and can be made suitable for all ages by changing the value and intensity.
Explain the three characteristics of colour.
(i) Hue is the name of the colour such as red or blue. (ii) Value is its lightness or darkness (tints and shades). (iii) Intensity is its brightness or dullness.
List the factors influencing the use of colours with examples (three points).

(i) Age and sex: bright colours for children and young adults. (ii) Occasion and season: cool, soft colours in summer; bright and dark colours in winter. (iii) Type of garment, profession and body structure.
Explain the meaning of any three colours.
(i) Red denotes love, health and vitality (dark) or passion and danger (bright). (ii) Blue denotes calmness, sincerity and idealism. (iii) Purple denotes magnificence and royalty.
la: Explain the different colour schemes with examples.

(i) Monochromatic: tints and shades of one colour. (ii) Analogous: neighbouring colours, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. (iii) Complementary: opposite colours, such as red and green. (iv) Split complementary: yellow with red-purple and blue-purple. (v) Triad: three colours forming an equilateral triangle, such as red, yellow and blue. (vi) Tetrad: four colours forming a square, used in Kashida, Kantha and Chamba Rumal.
